structure.overview: Mr. Lam, the applicant, challenged a decision of the Law Society of Ontario (LSO), the respondent, alleging fraud and seeking damages. The Federal Court reviewed the motion to strike Mr. Lam's claim, finding it disclosed no reasonable cause of action and was vexatious. The Court struck the claim without leave to amend and awarded costs to the LSO.

party_points.text: Claim attacks T-1394-23 Decision as fabricated and alleges LSO fraud
LSO requests costs on substantial indemnity basis and high end of Tariff B
ITO test for jurisdiction involves three steps including federal law essential to case
Windsor clarifies ITO test applies to claim's essential nature, here breach of contract

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Lam was served with the LSO's motion record and was aware of the motion scheduled for February 14, 2024, as confirmed by service certificate and his emails.
idea_list: Mr. Lam aware of motion and date

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: A Direction was issued on February 12, 2024, as a result of emails Mr. Lam sent to the Registry regarding the LSO's motion.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Lam received the Direction and sent an email on February 13, 2024, alleging fraud and impersonation related to the Direction and motion hearing.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Despite notice of the motion and hearing date, Mr. Lam did not attend, request adjournment, file a respondent's record, or request an extension.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The motion hearing proceeded on February 13, 2024, without Mr. Lam's attendance.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Lam's Claim attacks the T-1394-23 Decision as fabricated and alleges the LSO committed fraud by publishing fake judgments, seeking $480,000 and punitive damages.
idea_list: Allegations of LSO fraud and fake judgments

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Justice Gleeson explained that allegations based on speculation or that are scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious need not be accepted as true on a motion to strike.

citations.why: Explains exceptions to accepting allegations as true
Supports exception to accepting allegations as true
Supports exception to accepting allegations as true

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Although the LSO filed no evidence, the law on considering documents referred to in pleadings is briefly set out, citing Bouchard v. Canada.

citations.why: Explains law on documents referred to in pleadings

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court reviewed and considered the T-1394-23 Decision attached to the Claim for the motion under Rules 221(1)(a) and (c).

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The law on motions to strike balances protecting plaintiffs' right to a hearing with avoiding burdening courts with doomed claims, using developed tests.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The test for a motion to strike requires the defendant to show it is plain and obvious the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action, assuming facts true.

citations.cite: R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42 at para 17
citations.why: Sets high bar for motion to strike

citations.cite: Hunt v Carey Canada Inc, [1990] 2 SCR 959 at p 980
citations.why: Supports test for motion to strike

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Facts in the statement of claim must be accepted as true unless clearly unprovable or speculative; claims are read generously, especially if self-represented.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The claim must set out facts supporting a recognized or considered cause of action, including all elements; novelty alone is not grounds to strike.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Justice Roy explained a statement of claim requires a clear story of material facts supporting specific allegations and causes of action.

citations.cite: Al Omani v. Canada, 2017 FC 786 at para 17
citations.why: Explains requirement for clear factual story in claim

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Flexibility for self-represented parties exists but does not excuse compliance with rules to ensure fairness and avoid vague or speculative claims.

citations.cite: Barkley v Canada, 2014 FC 39 at para 17
citations.why: Supports need for compliance despite self-representation

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Flexibility for self-representation cannot override justice and fairness demands for all parties, as ensured by rules and case principles.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Claim is struck because it discloses no reasonable cause of action due to lack of jurisdiction and is vexatious; either ground suffices.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Allegations of misrepresentation, fraud, or malice must be particularized; bald allegations are scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, and abuse of process.

citations.why: Requires particulars for serious allegations

citations.cite: Merchant Law Group v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2010 FCA 184 at paras 34-35
citations.why: Supports requirement for particulars and abuse of process finding

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Claim is struck without leave to amend.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The LSO requests costs on a substantial indemnity basis and at the high end of column IV of Tariff B for this motion.

citations.why: LSO requests costs based on Tariff B

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Costs of $2,000 are awarded to the LSO, payable by Mr. Lam forthwith, considering rules, LSO's success, and the vexatious nature of the Claim.

Factors for awarding costs

summaries.summary: Two Federal Court of Appeal decisions, Peter G. White and Air Muskoka, provide good summaries of the relevant law on jurisdiction.

citations.cite: Peter G. White Management Ltd. v. Canada (Minister of Canadian Heritage), 2006 FCA 190

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The ITO test for jurisdiction involves three steps: statutory grant, federal law essential to case, and valid federal law basis; breach of contract claims may satisfy step 2 if federal regulation applies.
idea_list: Application to breach of contract claims

citations.why: Sets three-part test for jurisdiction
Step 1 requires action created or recognized under federal law
Step 2 may be satisfied by federal regulatory scheme for contract claims

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Windsor clarifies the ITO test applies to the claim's essential nature, not its pleading form; here, the claim is essentially for breach of contract.

citations.why: ITO test applies to essential nature of claim
